metadata.scope: e_japan (all 237 baronies across k_azuma, k_hitakami, k_tsukushi, k_yamato)

schema_notes.is_historical_867: true if the barony name is attested as a settlement/fortress/administrative unit/shrine by <= 867 CE; false if first attested post-867 CE or unattested.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Tracks attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: true only when the toponym directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).

b_ibaraki.first_mention_attestation: Hitachi Fudoki (compiled 713–721 CE), recording Ubaraki-gun (茨城郡) and the earlier Ubaraki-no-kuni (茨城国).
b_ibaraki.etymology_analysis: Attested as Ubaraki-gun (茨城郡) in Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE), which derives the name from Old Japanese ubara ('thorny bramble') + ki ('palisade/fortress'), recounting that Kurosaka-no-mikoto built thorn barricades to subdue local Kuzu groups. Historical in 867 CE.

b_kashima_hitachi.first_mention_attestation: Hitachi Fudoki (compiled 713–721 CE) as Kashima-gun (香島郡) and Kashima-no-Ōkami; Shoku Nihongi (723 CE) uses the orthography 鹿島郡.
b_kashima_hitachi.etymology_analysis: Attested as Kashima-gun (香島郡) and its sacred shrine in Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE), and as 鹿島郡 in Shoku Nihongi (723 CE). The name combines Old Japanese ka (later reinterpreted as 'deer', 鹿) + shima ('island/peninsula'). Historical in 867 CE.

b_naka_hitachi.first_mention_attestation: Kojiki (712 CE) as Naka-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko (仲国造); Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE) as Naka-gun (那賀郡).
b_naka_hitachi.etymology_analysis: Attested in Kojiki (712 CE) via Naka-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko (仲国造) and in Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE) as Naka-gun (那賀郡), later also written 那珂郡. Derived from Old Japanese naka ('middle/center'), denoting its central position in Hitachi Province. Historical in 867 CE.

b_taga_hitachi.first_mention_attestation: Hitachi Fudoki (compiled 713–721 CE) as Taka-gun (多珂郡) and Taka-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko (多珂国造), later written 多賀郡.
b_taga_hitachi.etymology_analysis: Attested as Taka-gun (多珂郡) in Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE), later standardized with auspicious kanji as 多賀郡 (Taga-gun). Derived from Old Japanese taka ('high'), referring to the elevated terrain of northern Hitachi. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 多贺 (多賀) [MênichGluck] — Calque: Abundant + Auspicious congratulation

b_tsukuba.first_mention_attestation: Kojiki (712 CE) in Yamato Takeru's poem ('Niibari Tsukuba'); Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE) as Tsukuba-gun (筑波郡) and Mount Tsukuba (筑波岳).

natural_proper_name.name: Mount Tsukuba (筑波山 / 筑波岳)

b_tsukuba.etymology_analysis: Attested in Kojiki (712 CE) and as Tsukuba-gun (筑波郡) in Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE). The district takes its name directly from the sacred Mount Tsukuba (筑波岳 / 筑波山), whose name is traditionally linked to Old Japanese tsuku ('to build/pile up') or *tsuku-ba ('slope/peak'). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 筑波 [Boudwelle] — Calque: Constructed fortress + Water waves

b_ichihara.first_mention_attestation: Fujiwara-kyō wooden tablet (mokkan, 694–710 CE) inscribed '上総国市原郡市原郷〈市原郡市原里〉' (Kazusa Province, Ichihara District, Ichihara Village).
b_ichihara.etymology_analysis: Attested on a Fujiwara-kyō mokkan (694–710 CE) as Ichihara-gun (市原郡) in Kazusa Province, and later as the site of the Kazusa provincial capital in Wamyō Ruijūshō (938 CE). Composed of Old Japanese ichi ('market') + hara ('plain'). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 市原 [Marctveit] — Calque: Market town + High plateau plain

b_awa.first_mention_attestation: Shoku Nihongi (Monmu 4, 700 CE, second month) recording Awa-gun (安房郡) in Kazusa Province, later elevated to Awa Province (安房国) in 718 CE.
b_awa.etymology_analysis: Attested as Awa-gun (安房郡) in Shoku Nihongi (700 CE) and separated from Kazusa as Awa Province in 718 CE. According to Kogoshūi (807 CE), the name was brought by Inbe migrants from Awa (粟/阿波, 'millet') in Shikoku and written with auspicious ateji 安房. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 安房 [Fridkamer] — Calque: Pacified peace + Chamber

b_ichinomiya.first_mention_attestation: Late Heian / Kamakura records (e.g., 1182 CE votive document and Azuma Kagami) referring to Tamasaki Shrine as Kazusa-no-kuni Ichinomiya (上総国一宮); Tamasaki Shrine itself is first attested as Tamasaki-no-kami (玉崎神) in Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku in 868 CE.
b_ichinomiya.etymology_analysis: Means 'First Shrine' (一宮, Ichinomiya), referring to the highest-ranking shrine of Kazusa Province (Tamasaki Shrine, 玉前神社). The ichinomiya ranking system developed after 867 CE (10th–12th centuries), and even Tamasaki Shrine's earliest recorded attestation (玉崎神 in Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku, 868 CE) postdates 867 CE. Anachronistic for 867 CE.

b_katsushika.first_mention_attestation: Shōsōin Documents, Yōrō 5 (721 CE) household register for Shimōsa Province, Katsushika District, Ōshima Township (下総国葛飾郡大嶋郷養老五年戸籍).
b_katsushika.etymology_analysis: Attested in the 721 CE Shōsōin household register as Katsushika-gun (葛飾郡) and in Man'yōshū (c. 759 CE) as Kadushika. Written with kanji for 'kudzu' + 'adorn', likely phonetic ateji for an older wetland/sandbar toponym. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 葛饰 (葛飾) [KudzuZier] — Calque: Kudzu vine + Adorn

b_katori.first_mention_attestation: Hitachi Fudoki (compiled 713–721 CE) as Katori (香取); Nihon Shoki (720 CE) as Kajitori (檝取) and Shōsōin (721 CE) as Katori-gun (釪托郡).
b_katori.etymology_analysis: Attested in Hitachi Fudoki (713–721 CE) as Katori and in Nihon Shoki (720 CE) as Kajitori (檝取), referring to Katori Shrine and Katori-gun in Shimōsa Province. Derived from Old Japanese *kaji-tori ('steersman/rudder-taker') or *katori ('fine silk'). Historical in 867 CE.

b_chiba.first_mention_attestation: Man'yōshū Vol. 20 (poem 20-4387, composed 755 CE by a sakimori from Chiba-gun, 千葉郡) and Heijō-kyō mokkan dated 792 CE (下総国千葉郡千葉郷).
b_chiba.etymology_analysis: Attested as Chiba-gun (千葉郡) in Man'yōshū Vol. 20 (755 CE) and on a 792 CE Heijō-kyō mokkan. Composed of Old Japanese chi ('thousand') + ha ('leaves'), meaning 'land of abundant foliage' (or phonetic for *chiwa). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: DûsentBlat
current_repo_state.b_origin: 千叶 (千葉) [DûsentBlat] — Calque: Thousand + Leaf

b_inba.first_mention_attestation: Man'yōshū Vol. 20 (poem 20-4389, composed 755 CE by Hasebe no Ōmaro of Iniwa-gun, 印波郡), later written Inba-gun (印旛郡).
b_inba.etymology_analysis: Attested as Iniwa-gun (印波郡) in Man'yōshū Vol. 20 (755 CE), evolving phonetically via nasalization (*iniwa > *inba) and later written 印旛郡 (Inba-gun). Phonetic kanji transcription of an ancient local toponym. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 印旛 [ZêgelVâne] — Calque: Imperial seal + Pennant

b_ashikaga.first_mention_attestation: Fujiwara-kyō wooden tablet (mokkan, 694–710 CE) inscribed '下毛野国足利郡波自可里' (Shimotsuke Province, Ashikaga District, Hajika Village).
b_ashikaga.etymology_analysis: Attested on a Fujiwara-kyō mokkan (694–710 CE) as Ashikaga-gun (足利郡) in Shimotsuke Province, long predating the medieval Ashikaga clan. Likely derived from Old Japanese *ashi ('reed' or 'foot') + *kaga ('slope/place'), written with auspicious kanji 足利. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: VûzWên
current_repo_state.b_origin: 足利 [VûzWên] — Calque: Foot + Advantage

b_futara.first_mention_attestation: Shoku Nihon Kōki (Jōwa 3, 836 CE, 12th month, 25th day) granting court rank to Futaara-no-kami (二荒神) in Shimotsuke Province.
b_futara.etymology_analysis: Attested in Shoku Nihon Kōki (836 CE) as Futaara-no-kami (二荒神) and in Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku (860 CE) as Futaara Shrine (二荒神社). Named after the sacred Mount Futara (二荒山, later also read Nikkō via Sino-Japanese on'yomi). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: TwêWiltberch
current_repo_state.b_origin: 二荒山 [TwêWiltberch] — Calque: Two + Wilderness + Mountain

b_nasu.first_mention_attestation: Nasu no Kuni no Miyatsuko Stele (那須国造碑, erected 700 CE), recording Nasu no Atai Ide and the Nasu district/polity in 689 CE.
b_nasu.etymology_analysis: Attested on the Nasu no Kuni no Miyatsuko Stele (700 CE) as Nasu (那須), corresponding to Nasu-gun (那須郡) in Shimotsuke Province. Phonetic kanji transcription of an ancient regional name (variously linked to *nasu 'slope/field' or Ainu/eastern-dialect substratum). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: NâBârt
current_repo_state.b_origin: 那须 (那須) [NâBârt] — Calque: Prefecture + Must

b_utsunomiya.first_mention_attestation: Late Heian / Kamakura sources: Utsunomiya (宇都宮) arose as the popular name (Utsunomiya Daimyōjin) of Futaarayama Shrine and the Utsunomiya clan founded by Fujiwara no Sōen (appointed shamushoku in 1063 CE; attested in Azuma Kagami in 1184 CE).
b_utsunomiya.etymology_analysis: The toponym Utsunomiya (宇都宮) is unattested by 867 CE; it emerged in the late Heian period (11th–12th centuries) from Utsunomiya Daimyōjin, a popular epithet for Futaarayama Shrine (二荒山神社, itself attested from 836 CE in Shoku Nihon Kōki), likely a phonetic shift from Ichinomiya ('First Shrine'). Anachronistic for 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Hûsstatpalz
current_repo_state.b_origin: 宇都宫 (宇都宮) [Hûsstatpalz] — Calque: Canopy + Great metropolis + Imperial palace

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Shoku Nihon Kōki (836 CE) as Futaara-no-kami (二荒神); Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku (860 CE) as Futaara Shrine (二荒神社).
older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to the late Heian emergence of the name Utsunomiya (11th–12th century), the shrine and site were documented as Futaara / Futaarayama Shrine.

b_shioya.first_mention_attestation: Engishiki (927 CE) recording Shioya-gun (塩屋郡) post-horse quotas in Shimotsuke Province, and Wamyō Ruijūshō (938 CE) glossed '志保之夜' (Shihonoya).
b_shioya.etymology_analysis: First attested in Engishiki (927 CE) and Wamyō Ruijūshō (938 CE) as Shioya-gun / Shionoya-gun (塩屋郡), later written 塩谷郡. No written attestation <= 867 CE survives. Composed of Japanese shio ('salt') + ya ('house/valley'). Anachronistic for 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Salzdal
current_repo_state.b_origin: 盐谷 (塩谷) [Salzdal] — Calque: Salt mineral brine + Mountain valley

b_kubiki.first_mention_attestation: Tōdaiji Documents (東大寺文書, Tenpyō-shōhō 5, 753 CE) recording estates in Kubiki-gun (頸城郡), Echigo Province (implied earlier in Shoku Nihongi 702 CE among four unnamed districts transferred from Etchū).
b_kubiki.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested as Kubiki-gun (頸城郡) in Tōdaiji estate records of 753 CE (Tenpyō-shōhō 5). Written with kanji for 'neck' + 'fortress/walled enclosure', likely reflecting an early frontier stronghold or coastal pass. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Halsburch
current_repo_state.b_origin: 颈城 (頸城) [Halsburch] — Calque: Neck isthmus (Kubiki) + Walled citadel

b_yahiko.first_mention_attestation: Man'yōshū Vol. 16 (compiled c. 759 CE, poems 16-3883 and 16-3884) praising the deity Iyahiko (伊夜比古); Shoku Nihon Kōki (833 CE) records Iyahiko-no-kami.

natural_proper_name.name: Mount Yahiko (弥彦山 / 伊夜比古山)

b_yahiko.etymology_analysis: Attested in Man'yōshū Vol. 16 (c. 759 CE) as Iyahiko (伊夜比古) and in Shoku Nihon Kōki (833 CE) as Iyahiko-no-kami. Derived from Old Japanese iya ('increasingly/great') + hiko ('prince/male deity'), naming both sacred Mount Yahiko and Yahiko Shrine at its foot. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: WeitEdel
current_repo_state.b_origin: 弥彦 [WeitEdel] — Calque: All-pervading + Virtuous nobleman

b_kambara.first_mention_attestation: Saidaiji Shizai Rukichō (780 CE) citing the 778 CE (Hōki 9) land survey of Uzurahashi-shō in Kambara-gun, Echigo Province (越後国蒲原郡).
b_kambara.etymology_analysis: Explicitly attested as Kambara-gun (蒲原郡) in the 778 CE survey recorded in Saidaiji Shizai Rukichō (780 CE). Derived from Old Japanese kama ('cattail/bulrush') + hara ('plain'), describing the marshy Echigo plain. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Lischtveit
current_repo_state.b_origin: 蒲原 [Lischtveit] — Calque: Cattail bulrush + High plateau plain

b_iwafune.first_mention_attestation: Nihon Shoki (compiled 720 CE), Taika 4 (648 CE) entry recording the construction of Iwafune Palisade (磐舟柵) in Echigo against the Emishi.
b_iwafune.etymology_analysis: Attested in Nihon Shoki for 648 CE as Iwafune Palisade (磐舟柵), later Iwafune-gun (岩船郡). Composed of Old Japanese iwa ('rock/crag') + fune ('boat/ship'), referring to rock formations or the legendary stone boat of Nigihayahi-no-mikoto. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 岩船 [Felsschif] — Calque: Crag + Ship

b_sado.first_mention_attestation: Shoku Nihongi (Monmu 4, 700 CE) recording Sado Province (佐渡国) alongside Echigo; Kojiki (712 CE) records Sado Island (佐度島) in the Kuniumi myth.

natural_proper_name.name: Sado Island (佐渡島 / 佐度島)

b_sado.etymology_analysis: Attested as Sado Province (佐渡国) in Shoku Nihongi (700 CE) and as Sado Island (佐度島) in Kojiki (712 CE). Named after the island choronym Sado, traditionally linked to *sa-to ('narrow strait/crossing') or *sawa-to ('many inlets'). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Helfvurt
current_repo_state.b_origin: 佐渡 [Helfvurt] — Calque: Counselor + Ferry crossing

b_uonuma.first_mention_attestation: Engishiki Jinmyōchō (927 CE) listing five shrines in Uonuma-gun (魚沼郡), Echigo Province, and Wamyō Ruijūshō (938 CE). (Shoku Nihongi 702 CE mentions four unnamed districts transferred from Etchū without naming Uonuma.)
b_uonuma.etymology_analysis: First explicitly attested by name in Engishiki (927 CE) and Wamyō Ruijūshō (938 CE) as Uonuma-gun (魚沼郡). Composed of Japanese uo ('fish') + numa ('marsh/swamp'). Because no <= 867 CE written source explicitly names Uonuma, it is marked anachronistic for 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Fischmôr
current_repo_state.b_origin: 鱼沼 (魚沼) [Fischmôr] — Calque: Fish + Swamp

b_nyu.first_mention_attestation: Heijō-kyō wooden tablets (mokkan, 710–717 CE) inscribed '越前国丹生郡朝津郷' / '賀茂郷' and Nagaya-ō-ke mokkan (714–715 CE, '丹生郡中山里').
b_nyu.etymology_analysis: Attested on Heijō-kyō mokkan (710–717 CE) and Nagaya-ō-ke mokkan (714–715 CE) as Nyu-gun (丹生郡) in Echizen Province. Derived from Old Japanese ni ('cinnabar/vermilion') + fu ('producing place'), denoting a cinnabar-yielding area. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.b_origin: 丹生 [ZinôberLêvende] — Calque: Cinnabar + Life renewal

b_ono_echizen.first_mention_attestation: Heijō-kyō wooden tablet (mokkan, following the Yōrō 6 / 722 CE chō-sen coin tax edict) inscribed '越前国大野郡', and Shoku Nihongi (797 CE).
b_ono_echizen.etymology_analysis: Attested on Nara-period Heijō-kyō mokkan (from 722 CE) as Ōno-gun (大野郡) in Echizen Province. Composed of Old Japanese ō ('great') + no ('plain/field'), describing the broad Ōno Basin. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Grôzfelt
current_repo_state.b_origin: 大野 [Grôzfelt] — Calque: Great + Open wilderness plain

b_tsuruga.first_mention_attestation: Nagaya-ō-ke wooden tablet (mokkan, 710–729 CE) inscribed '越前国敦賀郡' (Echizen Province, Tsuruga District); earlier orthography Tsunuga (角鹿) appears in Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE).
b_tsuruga.etymology_analysis: Attested as Tsuruga-gun (敦賀郡) on early Nara-period Nagaya-ō-ke mokkan (710–729 CE), evolving from the earlier form Tsunuga (角鹿) recorded in Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: TrouweGluck
current_repo_state.b_origin: 敦贺 (敦賀) [TrouweGluck] — Calque: Staunch + Auspicious congratulation

b_wakasa.first_mention_attestation: Fujiwara-kyō wooden tablet (mokkan, Monmu 4 / 700 CE) inscribed '庚子年四月／若佐国小丹生評', and Kojiki (712 CE) / Nihon Shoki (720 CE) as 若狭.
b_wakasa.etymology_analysis: Attested on a 700 CE Fujiwara-kyō mokkan as Wakasa Province (若佐国) and in Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE) as 若狭. The kanji 若狭 ('young + narrow') are phonetic ateji for an ancient regional name. Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: JuncEnge
current_repo_state.b_origin: 若狭 [JuncEnge] — Calque: Young + Narrow pass

b_sakai.first_mention_attestation: Heijō-kyō wooden tablet (mokkan, 765–770 CE) inscribed '越前国坂井郡' and Tōdaiji estate map (東大寺開田図) dated Tenpyō-jingo 2 (766 CE, '越前国坂井郡高串村').
b_sakai.etymology_analysis: Attested on Heijō-kyō mokkan (765–770 CE) and the 766 CE Tōdaiji Kaidenzu estate map as Sakai-gun (坂井郡) in Echizen Province. Composed of Old Japanese saka ('slope/hill') + i ('well/spring'). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Leitebrunn
current_repo_state.b_origin: 坂井 [Leitebrunn] — Calque: Mountain slope + Well

b_imizu.first_mention_attestation: Man'yōshū Vol. 17 (746–751 CE) in Ōtomo no Yakamochi's poems on Imizu-gun (射水郡), and Tōdaiji estate map dated Tenpyō-hōji 3 (759 CE, '越中国射水郡鳴戸村墾田図').
b_imizu.etymology_analysis: Attested in Man'yōshū Vol. 17 (746–751 CE) and on the 759 CE Tōdaiji estate map as Imizu-gun (射水郡), seat of the Etchū provincial capital. Derived from Old Japanese i-mizu ('spouting water/spring') or imitsu ('sacred water/port'). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Schützenwazzer
current_repo_state.b_origin: 射水 [Schützenwazzer] — Calque: Archery + Freshwater

b_tateyama.first_mention_attestation: Man'yōshū Vol. 17, 'Tateyama no Fu' (立山の賦) by Ōtomo no Yakamochi, explicitly dated Tenpyō 19, 4th month, 27th day (747 CE), praising Mount Tateyama as a sacred mountain.
b_tateyama.etymology_analysis: Attested in Man'yōshū Vol. 17 (747 CE) as Tachiyama / Tateyama (立山), revered as a sacred kami mountain in Etchū Province. Composed of Old Japanese tachi/tate ('standing upright') + yama ('mountain'). Historical in 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Stantberch
current_repo_state.b_origin: 立山 [Stantberch] — Calque: Stand upright + Mountain

b_enuma.first_mention_attestation: Shosoin Monjo, 'Echizen no Kuni Enuma-gun Yamashiro-go Keicho' (Tenpyo 12, 740 CE); Enuma-gun was formed in 701 CE from the 7th-century Yono-kohori (与野評).
b_enuma.etymology_analysis: Enuma (江沼, Old Japanese Enu/Enuma) is a descriptive topographic compound combining 'e' (inlet/river) and 'numa' (marsh/lagoon), referring to the coastal lagoons of southern Kaga. Pre-Ritsuryo pottery from Natakonpirayama attests Yono-kohori (与野評) in the 7th century, which became Enuma-gun under the Taiho Code (701 CE) and is explicitly dated in the 740 CE Shosoin census register; Nomi-gun was split from it in 823 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Flôzmôr
current_repo_state.b_origin: 江沼 [Flôzmôr] — Calque: Major southern river + Swamp

b_haku.first_mention_attestation: Nihon Montoku Tenno Jitsuroku (Ninju 3, 853 CE, 10th month): first court rank (Junior Third Rank) granted to Shirayama-hime-no-kami (白山比咩神) of Mount Haku (Hakusan).
b_haku.etymology_analysis: Haku (白山, Hakusan / Shirayama) directly adopts the oronym of Mount Haku, one of Japan's Three Sacred Mountains, so named for its year-round snow cover. Shugenja tradition dates its opening by Taicho to 717 CE, and its tutelary deity Shirayama-hime-no-kami is first attested in the imperial chronicles in 853 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Wîzberch
current_repo_state.b_origin: 白山 [Wîzberch] — Calque: White + Mountain
